segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: New York City, the Port Authority Bus Terminal, a very cold night, a few weeks ago--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, explain what time it is, and where we are and what we're doing.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: It is 11:14 PM. And we are waiting for a Texas bus.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Texas bus with who inside?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: So we don't know the number yet, but we have asylum seekers that are there that just come from the border.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is one of the buses that Governor Greg Abbott sent to New York City, starting in the summer of last year. You probably heard about this. Hoping to make a point about what Texas is dealing with, he sent migrants on buses to cities run by Democrats-- Washington, DC, Los Angeles, Chicago, Philadelphia, Denver, and New York.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Over 27,000 people have arrived at this spot this way, where many of them have been greeted by a 5'2" Black woman, named Adama Bah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: How many nights a week do you do this?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: Mm. I don't keep count anymore. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But what's the most it gets? Like, what's a hard week for you?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: A hard week is every day, a bus. I put the kids to sleep, and then I ran over here. I'm a mommy. And I'll make it back in time, where they won't notice I'm gone.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do they know you left?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Thing is, Adama doesn't work for the city of New York. She runs a community center for newly arrived immigrants, called Afrikana. She's been doing this work with migrants for 18 years-- for a long time, just out of her car, though she still does a lot of work from her car, going around a city to where recent migrants are, talking to them in the car.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: My car has been my office for years, and it's still my office.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And are there certain things you always are sure that you keep in the car?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: I have so many stuff. So organizer 101 is always have a portable charger, paper and pen. I have toothbrush, toothpaste-- peppermint, because I'm always talking to people. I don't think-- I don't want to be known as the lady with the bad breath.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: She can help you, but she has a bad breath. I have deodorant, emergency change of clothes. Because sometimes-- it's not on purpose, but I spend overnight.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Have you had to sleep overnight here, waiting for buses?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: Yeah, I have. I have pillows. I have a blanket.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When the very first bus arrived from Texas in August 2022, it was migrant aid groups like Adama's who got advance word that it was coming and greeted the bus-- not the city. But soon enough, the city government got on board. Mayor Eric Adams showed up at the Port Authority to greet one of the buses, ready to prove that New York City is a city of immigrants that loves and welcomes immigrants.

segments.speaker: Eric Adams
segments.text: I have to provide services for families that are here, and that's what we're going to do, and that's what our responsibility as a city-- I'm proud that this is a right-to-shelter state.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Right to shelter-- that means that New York City had to provide temporary housing to anyone who needs it. And the city took that seriously.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: They started to show up. They set up operations.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And where did the city do its operation? What was it?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: Inside there in Port Authority.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Right through those doors here?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: Right through those doors.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: On that spot, the city would take people's names and information, and then send them on to shelters. Groups like Adama's would hand out food, clothing, toiletries. As word got out that New York City would house everyone who showed up, more and more people started arriving.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today, the 27,000 people that Governor Abbott sent are just a tiny portion of the 150,000 who've shown up on buses, trains, cars, and planes since the spring of 2022. New York City was not set up to help this many people this way. The right to shelter was created for homeless men in the Bowery, not for thousands of new arrivals each week.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: By this fall, it was costing the city $10 million a night, and the mayor completely changed his tune. Yes, New York loves immigrants, but not this many this fast, needing assistance. And the mayor became a kind of one-man unwelcome wagon, flying to Ecuador and Colombia and Mexico to hold press conferences saying, don't come to New York, declaring a state of emergency in the city, begging the federal government for help, which did not arrive.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: By October of this year, the city had spent over $2 billion and opened over 200 emergency shelters. It had cut the amount of time that immigrants could stay in a shelter from as long as they needed to 60 days for families and 30 days for individuals. And finally, in October, New York went to court to change the law and suspend the right to shelter for the city. Mayor Adams started saying that migrants will be sleeping on the streets. It's not a question of if, but when.

segments.speaker: Eric Adams
segments.text: We're getting 10,000 migrants a month.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is Mayor Adams this fall.

segments.speaker: Eric Adams
segments.text: This issue will destroy New York City, destroy New York City. Every community in this city is going to be impacted. We have a $12 billion deficit that we're going to have to cut. Every service in this city is going to be impacted, all of us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Or maybe it's not quite that bad. The city's chief fiscal officer, the comptroller, says the mayor is overblowing the effects of the migrants on the city's budget. And one political question in New York is whether the mayor is now scapegoating the migrants to push through budget cuts he'd hoped to do anyway. Though it is true that money is tight, one day, Adama says, city personnel just didn't show up at Port Authority anymore to greet immigrants.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: They just stopped. They didn't tell us that they were stopping. They-- the same day, they just told us they were closing operations. They didn't give us a reason. They didn't give us-- they didn't work with us. They didn't give us a heads-up. They just shut it down.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Which brings us to why Adama's here, where her kids are with her parents at home, sleeping. If she weren't here, this bus that's arriving from Texas would drop off a few dozen people in this alley between 41st and 42nd Street. A couple National Guardsmen would sleepily emerge from the car they're sitting in across the street and hand out an address to go to and a map. And they'd have to make their way there on their own.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The address is for the Roosevelt Hotel, which the city has set up as the intake center for migrants arriving in New York. 20-minute walk from here, right through the center of Times Square.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: So we're here to welcome them, and then actually safely send them there.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Adama's organization partnered with another organization to hire a bus.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: So what I'm going to do is put them in the bus and send them straight to the Roosevelt, and tell them, please give them food right now. And then, they will give them sandwiches and water. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The other thing she's going to do is get on the bus and give them a little speech. The bus driver will translate to Spanish. The speech is partly practical. She gives out a phone number they type in their cell phones for somebody they can call once they're in a shelter, to direct them to the services they need.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But also, she's doing this herself, the head of the organization in the middle of the night, bus after bus, because she thinks it's important that somebody says "welcome," just in some basic human way, to people who have come so far, full of worry and fear and hope.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: So as a former asylum seeker, I didn't get that welcome party. My parents didn't get that welcome party. So I am doing it for them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But the thing you say is-- just so I understand, so the thing you're going to say is what? Give me the speech.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: So the first step is "Bienvenidos a Nueva York. You are in New York City, in Manhattan, in Port Authority. We want to welcome you. We're going to count you, and we're going to put you in another bus and transport you to Roosevelt Hotel, where there's a bathroom, there's water, there's food, and there's Wi-Fi." The Wi-Fi always gets them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She tells them that her organization can help with clothing and legal aid and anything else they need help with.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: And then we tell them, listen, this is a country of immigrants. I am an immigrant. I am from Africa. I am from Guinea. I'm an immigrant just like you.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: I made it, and you will make it. It's not easy in the beginning, but it will get better. You're welcome here. No matter what anybody tells you, you have rights. Practice those rights. If you don't know what they are, we will tell you what they are. And then, we let them out.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, time check-- what time is it?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: 11:50. It should be pulling up. Do you want a peppermint? No?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: Oh. Here you go.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Thanks.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We've been standing in the cold for over an hour. Random people walk up to Adama to start conversations or ask for directions. She just seems like the kind of person you can do that with. At around quarter past midnight, she reveals something that I can't believe I'm learning after standing there so long together.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: I have my pajamas on. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (LAUGHING) What?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: This is my pajamas.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Are you serious?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: I am.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, my god. It's true. Those are checked, teal-and-navy pajamas.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: I know. And I was like, ah, I don't feel like dressing up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so you're wearing a maroon coat and teal-and-navy pajamas, dark-blue hijab, backpack--

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: I'm ready to walk the runway. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Exactly.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Finally, more than an hour after that, 1:30 in the morning, the bus from Texas rolls up.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: OK. You cannot go inside, so you just have to wait here.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The bus door opens. She climbs the steps and stands at the front of the bus and makes her speech, which does the job. When everybody emerges from the bus after their three-day ride, they are not the exhausted, huddled masses that I expected they'd be. People are beaming, excited.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: Hola, bienvenidas. Fila por favor.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Some carry suitcases. Some carry plastic garbage bags filled with their stuff. In my terrible high-school Spanish, I ask where they're from. And families look so happy when they answer.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: De donde viene?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Venezuela.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Venezuela.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Venezuela? De donde viene?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Honduras.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Honduras.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: Colombia.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Y de donde?

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: Colombia.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Colombia?

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Venezuela.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Venezuela.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They tell me they've been traveling for a month and a half, two months, three months. It's a dangerous trip for many of them through the Darien Gap. Most are from Venezuela, a lot of Colombia. Plus, one family where the dad proudly shouted his answer like, I don't know about these people, but I definitely belong here.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: De donde?

segments.speaker: Speaker 9
segments.text: De Mexico! Viva Mexico!

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That guy has family in New York, who are on their way to come pick him up. Most everybody else got into the other bus Adama arranged and headed over to the migrant welcome center at the Roosevelt Hotel, a once-glamorous 1,000-room behemoth that fills a block of 45th Street, a place where, back in the day, you might spot JFK or Eisenhower or Guy Lombardo, that is now the city's new Ellis Island, the entrance point.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: Salida por favor.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Adama guides everyone off the bus into the lobby.

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: Hola. Entra. Entra por favor. Familia?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: How much Spanish do you speak now?

segments.speaker: Adama Bah
segments.text: None. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The welcome center at the Roosevelt Hotel is one part of the city's response. It's pretty well run. They have legal services to help you apply for asylum. There are free diapers and warm food.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They'll replace your meds. The city started doing this when a kid showed up whose meds for epilepsy had been seized by border patrol. And from here, they'll send you to one of the over 200 shelters around the city, which are mostly not as nice as this.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Some are in school gymnasiums, office buildings. If you have family elsewhere in the country, there's a desk here where New York City will happily buy you a plane ticket to go live with them and not be New York's problem anymore. 1/4 of the arrivals take that option.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As this year ends, New York City is entering some new phase with this massive experiment at welcoming and providing services for so many new arrivals. It's put some 20,000 kids into schools. It's housing right now 60,000 migrants.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Though in lots of ways, it has not gone so well, it hasn't put newcomers on a path to jobs and places to live. But has any American city ever done this much for new arrivals on this scale? Mayor Adams has pointed out some cities do nothing. Texas, Governor Abbott, does nothing.

segments.speaker: Eric Adams
segments.text: I was on the border in El Paso! I saw what happened with people and children and families sleeping in airports, sleeping on the street! So don't critique what we've done! Don't tell us how we could have done it better!

segments.speaker: Eric Adams
segments.text: Our hearts are big, but our resources are not endless. The way goes New York goes America. And if we don't get it right in New York City, we're not going to get it right in America.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our show, we look at a city desperately trying to prove that it can be the sanctuary city it thinks it is. We look at the messy, flawed, generous, impossible, vast New York migrant experiment, how it's going, where it works, and where it fails so badly that people have accused New York of deliberately doing horribly so immigrants decide not to stay in the city, what it's like to arrive here and make your way right now in New York. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 1, No Sleep Till Brooklyn. So let's start with what's probably the most difficult thing New York City has faced with these new migrants-- figuring out where to house them. It's hard to find appropriate spaces. And some neighborhoods really don't want them.

segments.speaker: Protesters
segments.text: Shut it down! Shut it down!

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Send them back home!

segments.speaker: Protesters
segments.text: Shut it down!

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is Staten Island, living up to every stereotype New Yorkers have about Staten Island when a migrant shelter got put there. There have also been protests in Brooklyn and Queens. With that in mind, the city opened up a new facility a month ago that the mayor said was chosen to be, quote, "the least intrusive as possible to current residents, while also being as humane as possible to migrants."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It is not in a building. It's four massive tents that, together, can house 2,000 people at a place called Floyd Bennett Field. One of our producers, Valerie Kipnis, visited right after it opened.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: When I first heard that Floyd Bennett Field was going to be the city's newest migrant center, it struck me, because I knew exactly where it was-- in the middle of nowhere. And I can say that with some degree of certainty, because I grew up in the same middle of nowhere-- or at least close by.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: It's called Floyd Bennett Field. But to me, it's always been the abandoned airport, slash place with the massive ice hockey rink, slash random chunk of land you pass just before Rockaway Beach. It's right on the water. There's not a lot of streetlights or ways to get there, unless you're in a car or on a bike.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And if you're driving around at night, it feels like you're in the middle of the woods, not New York City. I wondered what it was like to get sent there as someone brand new to the city. So I went out with Jika Gonzalez. She's a reporter I've worked with before, who covers immigration.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: We arrived at around dusk. There was the faint glow of cop cars near a massive encampment lit up by fluorescent lights. And there were the tents, surrounded by a giant metal fence and security guards.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Jika and I arrived unannounced, hoping to talk to people hanging out around the shelter. But that night was actually so cold that there was basically no one outside, except for this one group of adults with some kids. The kids wore blankets over their heads, trailing on the ground behind them, cute, but cold, like little ghosts. And actually, they were on their way out, in a rush.

segments.speaker: Jika Gonzalez
segments.text: Hola, que tal?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Why are you leaving here right now?

segments.speaker: Jika Gonzalez
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Rafael
segments.text: Nos estamos yendo de nuevo a la 45.

segments.speaker: Jika Gonzalez
segments.text: Trying to go to 45th Street.

segments.speaker: Child
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: What's on 45th Street?

segments.speaker: Jika Gonzalez
segments.text: Qué hay en la

segments.speaker: Child
segments.text: El hotel. Si.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: The Roosevelt Hotel, back to the welcome center. The little girl's name is Karlina, but she goes by Karli. She's eight, has big-sister energy, pigtails that some wisps of hair have escaped from. She rocks back and forth from heel to toe as she talks.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Her family arrived here only a few hours ago. And now, they're leaving, because this place isn't what they thought it would be.

segments.speaker: Roni
segments.text: Aqui nos habian dicho que nos

segments.speaker: Roni
segments.text: iban a mandar para un hotel y no era un hotel. Mira es una--un acampamento donde estamos todos durmiendo en camillas pues, entonces nosotros también necesitamos una privacidad para los niños. Si me entiende?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: "They said they were going to send us to a hotel, but it wasn't a hotel. It's a campsite," says one of the men, "where we're all sleeping on cots. And we need our privacy for the kids. You understand? And the bathrooms-- they're not in the main tent. You have to go outside to use them."

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Sometime along the way, they began to wonder about public transportation. How are the kids going to get to school from here? The closest train station is over 4 miles away. Rafael, Karlina's dad, is like, how will I find work from here?

segments.speaker: Rafael
segments.text: Entonces por una de esas cosas que nosotros buscamos refugio aquí para luego nosotros empezar a trabajar. Ganar nuestro dinero como ustedes también los Americanos.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: "That's why we're looking for shelter, so that way, we can start working, earning our own money, like you. That way, we can rent a house and take care of our expenses, you understand? They told us we were coming to a hotel, but then suddenly, when we were on the way here, we realized that this is like a desert, an island in the middle of nowhere."

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: The city says it shows people photos of the tents and maps of where they'll be going. But I later talked to other people here, and no one I spoke to had been shown photos. Lots of them were surprised when they arrived.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Karlina, her dad, Rafael, and the whole family, basically, as soon as they arrived, started thinking, we can't stay here. There has to be something else. Rafael seemed determined. He wanted to talk to the person who assigned them here, someone at the Roosevelt Hotel on 45th Street. They needed to get back.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: This group-- turns out there are two families from Venezuela, the capital, Caracas. A mom named Daniela, her husband Rafael, also her brother Roni and his family, and two other guys who they met along the way. Consider their journey up to this point, the one that got them to these giant tents in the middle of an abandoned airfield.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: They left Caracas in late summer, and for three months, made their way through Central America to Mexico, to Piedras Negras, and then into Texas. After they crossed, they were offered a choice of three buses-- Chicago, Denver, or New York. They knew Venezuelans in New York City who said they could get help here, that the kids could go to school, that the adults could find work. So they chose New York.

segments.speaker: Daniela
segments.text: Decidimos venirnos para acá, pero resulta que aquí ahora nos salieron con otra cosa.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Daniela, Karli's mom, says they were told they'd get a place to live for two months. "We could rest and look for work to move forward, you understand? So we decided to come to New York, because we'd get help here. But here, it is something else. Here has been confusing."

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: You arrive at the Roosevelt Hotel in the middle of the city, with a warm lobby, the breakfast, the bag check, the shelter assignment, the moment of stillness after months of chaos. And then, you get put on this bus, and it starts driving you away from the place you've been imagining, away from all the skyscrapers.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And suddenly, you're in this other place, far away from the crowds of Grand Central. And then, you get off the bus, and you're processed in a place that looks very much like a tent. Because it is a tent. It is something else.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: So the family had decided to leave and somehow try to make it back to 45th Street. The only way out seemed to be a city bus in a kind of parking lot. The neon sign scrolling across its front read "not in service." There was a man nearby in a Transit Authority uniform with a walkie talkie who seemed stressed out by the whole situation.

segments.speaker: Bus Driver
segments.text: I got, like, 15 people here that wants to get on the bus, but none of them speak English. I can't figure out where they want to go. I cannot go off route, right?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: While he's talking, he starts walking towards the parked bus. So the group decides they better follow him. They have almost no belongings, just a few plastic bags of stuff. The kids run ahead.

segments.speaker: Children
segments.text: Bye! Bye! Bye-bye! Ciao!

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: The kids climb onto the bus, go to the back. Some of them lay down. They look exhausted, sleepy. The adults have no idea what's going on, where the bus is going or anything. They crowd near the entrance of the bus.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: There's another bus driver already on board. The bus driver with the walkie talkie gets on as well. Neither of them speak Spanish. It falls to Jika to translate for them.

segments.speaker: Jika Gonzalez
segments.text: Sir? Sorry, they're just asking me where the bus is taking them.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: It's really unclear what's happening. I later learned that this is a new bus the city set up to shuttle people from the shelter to a subway station. But at this moment, in the first days of the shelter's operation, the driver seems a bit unsure about where he's going. He starts looking through his paperwork.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yes, Coney Island. Coney Island is not near 45th Street in the center of Manhattan. It's in the opposite direction.

segments.speaker: Bus Driver
segments.text: So it's going to Coney Island by the train.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: So you're only taking them to the train station?

segments.speaker: Bus Driver
segments.text: Correct.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: What if they want to go to the-- I think they're trying to go to the Roosevelt Hotel on 45th Street.

segments.speaker: Bus Driver
segments.text: I can't go off route.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Bus Driver
segments.text: That's my instructions.

segments.speaker: Jika Gonzalez
segments.text: I'm going to translate for them, is that OK? Ustedes están en una parte de Nueva York. Nueva York se llama Brooklyn. Y donde ustedes quieren ir es en Manhattan. Son como dos condados diferentes. Haz de cuenta. Aquí se llaman boroughs.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Jika's trying her best to explain to them in Spanish what he means. She's like, you're in a part of New York that is called Brooklyn, and where you're trying to go is Manhattan. It's two different counties. They're called boroughs here.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: They ask Jika, how are we supposed to transfer or pay for a train? We just got to the city. We have no money. The family keeps asking to go to 45th Street, the same way they got here, and the driver keeps repeating he can't go off route, that he can only take them to Coney Island, nowhere near where they want to go.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So once migrants get into the shelters that New York is providing, lots of them have no idea what they're supposed to do next or who to talk to. In theory, they all have case managers. segments.text: So there are all kinds of nonprofits trying to fill the gaps. segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then a woman opens the door and welcomes us. Hi.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Hi, you guys.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: I'm just a journalist who walked with them over from the thing.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She has some important information to share with everyone, but she doesn't speak French. So I translate.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I'm going to welcome them for five days. Monday morning, they go back to Afrikana.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: Five days, that's it. I feel terrible communicating this to the boys. This is not going to be their new home. And every day, they have to clear out of here from 8:00 AM to 8:00 PM.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: One of her boys mouths to me, [SPEAKING FRENCH], it's crazy. I don't know what to tell him. I kind of agree.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: I thought that when I went to Afrikana, I'd be taking a look at a sort of safety net under the city's safety net, a place that was catching all these people the city maybe wasn't. But that safety net has holes in it. For all the work Adama and her volunteers put in, it feels like it all comes down to luck.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: In the weeks that followed, I got texts and calls from a couple of the boys. They told me that they hadn't gotten placed in a long-term youth facility, that instead, they doubled down on staying in the city's regular migrant shelters.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: Adama told me it used to be easier to place young people. I happened to be there in late October, right when it started to become almost impossible. The youth shelter system is full.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: For weeks, I didn't hear anything from Lamine. But when I did get in touch with him, he told me he's staying at Covenant House, the big youth shelter Adama says is one of the best. He says he got the address off someone he met that day at Afrikana, and he took it from there. I got in here myself, he told me.

segments.speaker: Lamine
segments.text: [SPEAKING FRENCH]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Every day at 6:00 AM, I got up to go to Covenant House to ask if they have a place. They told me there is no place, so I came back. The next day, they said they still didn't have a place, but that maybe if I came back there, it might be a spot. So I kept going day after day. And then they told me they had a spot.

segments.speaker: Lamine
segments.text: [SPEAKING FRENCH]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: I did it. Not with the help of Afrikana. I did it alone. Just me.

segments.speaker: Lamine
segments.text: [SPEAKING FRENCH]

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: You can hear it, right, the pride in his voice? And he should be proud.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: He didn't get into one of Covenant House's two-year programs. But they did give him a spot for 60 days. He's going to school, learning English slowly. He's still sussing out how I can be useful, I think. Lately when we've talked, he's had a few questions for me about my own immigration story, how I came here.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: Adama told me she has a lot of Lamines, people who figure it out on their own. That was her goal when she first opened Afrikana. She'd help folks, and they'd be gone because she'd have connected them to the right people. But she's serving hundreds of people a day because so many of them end up returning. And so many more keep arriving.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: The night I came home from Afrikana after 10 hours with her, I'd been in bed about an hour when I got a call from Adama. There are buses on the way that she was meeting that night. Starting the whole thing all over again.
